subtitulo: Land, mountain, honor, and violence in the four centuries national history did not want to tell (1500 – 1800)

coda.heading: Coda for the journey: what to look at

items.text: First, the vocabulary. Everyday Greek is full of Turkish: the word for fork, for pillow, for coffee, for many dishes. And the food itself — yogurt, stuffed eggplant, kebab, baklava — is the object of national ownership disputes between Greece and Turkey taken very seriously indeed. Listen to those arguments: they are the same phenomenon as the dispute over pisco, and they reveal that an identity border is defended with more ferocity the more one resembles one's neighbor. Freud called it the narcissism of small differences; political sociology calls it ethnic boundary construction.

Second, in Athens, the Museum of Greek Folk Art and the Benaki Museum. There lies what the classical narrative leaves out: textiles, regional costumes, silverware, post-Byzantine icons, instruments. It is the material archive of those supposedly empty four centuries, and for a sociologist it is more informative than the Acropolis, because it shows how people lived, not how the nation wanted to remember itself.

Third, a contrast that only your itinerary allows. Corfu had no Ottoman çiftlik: it had a Venetian latifundium with a registered nobility. In both cases, peasants handing over a share of the harvest to an absentee owner; in one case the owner was a Muslim agha, in the other a Catholic count with a palace in the city. When someone explains to you that the islands' history was gentler because it was Western, keep in mind that sharecropping is sharecropping in any language. The real difference lies not in the degree of exploitation but in which national narrative was built afterward around each experience.

sections.heading: How a period gets erased
paragraphs: Greek national historiography baptized the years between 1453 and 1821 as TOURKOKRATIA, Turkish rule, and with that name it solved the problem of what to do with them: nothing happened, or what happened was undifferentiated suffering. Four centuries — more time than separates us from Cervantes — turned into a parenthesis between classical Greece and modern Greece. Naming a period after its foreign ruler is a political decision: it implies that the population was not the subject of its own history during that span.

The operation served a precise function in the nineteenth century. A new state claiming descent from Pericles needed the interval to be irrelevant, because any acknowledgment of Ottoman continuity in institutions, customs, cuisine, music, or vocabulary weakened the claim to Europeanness. That is why the new state undertook a linguistic purge — KATHAREVOUSA, Greek artificially cleansed of Turkish, Italian, and Slavic loanwords, imposed as the official language until 1976 — and an architectural purge, that of the minarets and the Frankish towers we already discussed.

The equivalent Peruvian operation is the construction of the colonial period as darkness between Inca splendor and the republic. There too a new state needed a noble past and a disposable interval, and there too what had lasted longest was erased. And in both cases the erasure fails at the same point: popular culture does not obey. The bouzouki, rebetiko, coffee, yogurt, everyday Greek vocabulary are full of the Ottoman, just as Peruvian Spanish, food, festivity, and religiosity are full of the colonial. Really existing identity is always more impure than the official one.

sections.heading: From tax assignment to estate: how the countryside got worse
paragraphs: The classic Ottoman agrarian regime was organized into TIMARS: the state did not grant land but the right to collect revenue from it, in exchange for cavalry service. The peasant was a hereditary usufructuary and not a serf, and the timariot was not an owner. Compared with the serfdom of contemporary Eastern Europe, the position of the sixteenth-century Balkan peasant was, in several respects, better.

What matters is what happens afterward. Between the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, with the empire's fiscal crisis and the expansion of tax farming — the iltizam and later the malikâne, a lifetime concession — the tax collectors effectively turned into landowners, and the ÇIFTLIK appeared: large private estates oriented toward exporting wheat and cotton to Western Europe, with peasants reduced to sharecroppers who handed over between a third and half the harvest. The phenomenon was especially intense in Thessaly and Macedonia, the fertile plains.

The sequence deserves underlining because it contradicts common sense: the condition of the Greek peasantry was not worse at the empire's height but during its DECLINE. When the central state weakens, it does not liberate the population: it leaves it at the mercy of the local powers that seize the fiscal function. A strong state can be oppressive, but a weak state usually means extraction is privatized and loses all limit. This is one of the most transferable lessons of the period, and it describes with precision the formation of the Peruvian hacienda: the most brutal latifundist expansion in the southern highlands did not occur under full colonial power but during the nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century republic, when the state was too weak to arbitrate and the gamonal filled that vacuum. José Carlos Mariátegui built his analysis of the "land problem" exactly on that observation.

sections.heading: What the village did on its own
paragraphs: Under indirect rule, Greek communities administered much of their own life. The KOCABAŞIS or proestoí — elected or co-opted local notables — divided the tax burden among families, settled disputes, and negotiated with the Ottoman authority. That system produced remarkable autonomies: the forty-six villages of Zagori, in Epirus, obtained fiscal privileges and nearly complete self-government; the mining communities of Chalkidiki managed their own production; Ambelakia, in Thessaly, organized in the late eighteenth century a cooperative for red-dyed thread that exported to Vienna and Leipzig with collective capital and management, and that astonished the European travelers who described it.

This is the central finding of social historiography over recent decades, and it is what disproves the empty parenthesis: there existed a dense local institutional life, with capacity for negotiation, accumulation, and outward projection. And its reverse existed too: that same system of intermediary notables, whose position depended on distributing burdens and favors, is the direct historical origin of modern Greek CLIENTELISM. The notable who in 1750 distributed the tax quota is the functional ancestor of the deputy who in 1980 secured a public-sector job. The structure survived the empire, the monarchy, the republic, and European integration, because it did not depend on the regime but on the relationship: access to resources mediated by a person, not guaranteed by a right. Peruvians need no translation for this.

In the mountains, the state simply did not reach. The Mani, in the Peloponnese, Sfakia in Crete, Souli in Epirus, functioned as zones of negotiated or nonexistent sovereignty, with armed clans, stone towers, and codified blood vengeance. And in the intermediate lands operated a fascinating institution: the ARMATOLOI, bandits whom the Ottoman state hired to control the other bandits, the KLEFTS. The border between the two was porous: the same man could be a bandit, then a guard, then a bandit again, depending on the negotiation. When 1821 arrives, those men will become the revolution's army and then, in the independent state, a public-order problem difficult to dissolve.

Classic Mediterranean anthropology — Campbell among the Sarakatsani in 1964, Peristiany's compilation on honor and shame in 1965 — built its model of honor as masculine social capital, with feminine shame as its counterpart, on the basis of these pastoral and mountain societies. That model has been rightly criticized as orientalist and for projecting onto the whole Mediterranean what was specific to particular communities. It is still worth retaining, however, as the description of a real mechanism: wherever the state does not guarantee security or justice, reputation fulfills that function, and its defense turns violent because effective protection depends on it. The same logic explains the peasant patrols of northern Peru and communal justice in the south: they are not cultural throwbacks, they are responses to the absence of the state.

sections.heading: The simultaneous world: the Qing, the Mughals, Túpac Amaru
paragraphs: The seventeenth and eighteenth centuries reorganize the entire world. The Qing dynasty replaces the Ming in 1644 and China reaches its greatest extent; the Mughal empire dominates India until the British East India Company begins to replace it after Plassey in 1757, in the first great demonstration that a mercantile corporation could conquer a subcontinent. Western Europe passes through the Thirty Years' War, the scientific revolution, and the Enlightenment, and emerges with fiscal-military states capable of extraction and mobilization that no traditional agrarian empire could match. That differential in state capacity, not cultural superiority, explains what will come in the nineteenth century.

In Peru, the eighteenth century is that of the Bourbon reforms — increased fiscal pressure, intendancies, the displacement of Creole elites — and of the greatest anticolonial rebellion in the Americas before the wars of independence: that of Túpac Amaru II in 1780–1781, followed by that of Túpac Katari in Upper Peru, with tens of thousands of dead. The subsequent repression abolished the curacazgos, banned the Comentarios Reales of Inca Garcilaso, prohibited the use of Inca titles and dress and theater in Quechua. In other words: the empire deliberately destroyed the memory and the intermediary institutions that it had itself recognized for two centuries.

Forty years later, the Ottoman Empire will do exactly the same to its own intermediary Greek elite, as we shall see in the next entry. The structural coincidence is notable: when a system of indirect government enters crisis, the center destroys the mediators it had relied on, and with them eliminates the only mechanism that had made domination tolerable. The most intense colonial violence tends to occur not at the height of dominance but at the moment dominance begins to fail.

sections.heading: Resonances 2024–2026: the emptying of the countryside and violence against women
paragraphs: Two legacies of this period are today at the center of Greek public debate. The first is demographic and territorial. The mountains and villages whose institutional life I have just described are today empty or converted into tourist heritage: Zagori has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2023, the Mani sells its towers as luxury lodgings, and Greece has one of the lowest birth rates in Europe and an accelerated aging that emigration in the 2010s aggravated. The Greek countryside is not in crisis: it is finished, and what remains of it is preserved as stage set. The Peruvian highlands are undergoing an equivalent process, with the difference that the migration was internal and produced Lima.

The second is violence. The honor model that anthropology described is not a museum object: it is the cultural substrate on which gender violence is debated today. In Greece, the term GYNAIKOKTONIA — femicide — burst into public debate from 2021 onward after a series of high-profile cases, and since then the feminist movement has demanded its autonomous criminalization, which successive governments have resisted, arguing that aggravated homicide already covers it; the debate remained open in 2025 and 2026. In Peru the path was the reverse and earlier: femicide has been an autonomous criminal offense since 2013, the 2016 Ni Una Menos mobilization was one of the largest in the country's history, and yet the numbers have not sustainably fallen. The comparison is instructive precisely because it shows the limits of the legal instrument: naming the crime is necessary and not sufficient, because what sustains the violence is a moral economy of honor and control that no law repeals by decree.

I suggest you observe this ethnographically and without condescension during the trip, because it is your craft and because Greece offers a dense case: watch who occupies the public space of a village square in the afternoon, who sits in the kafeneío, how the family table is organized in the taverna, who serves and who decides. And compare it with what you would see in Ayacucho or in Cajamarca. Not to conclude that they are the same — they are not — but to identify what varies and what does not.
